title: Basic Nursing Care — Oxygenation & Respiratory Care Basics (Set 9)
subtitle: Positioning for breathing, early vs late signs of hypoxia, oxygen delivery devices & safety, nasal-cannula skin care, pulse oximetry, incentive spirometry, pursed-lip breathing, secretion clearance and when to report respiratory distress
scenario: Supporting clients' oxygenation and breathing safely: positioning, recognizing hypoxia early, using oxygen equipment safely, basic pulmonary hygiene, and knowing which respiratory changes to report to the licensed nurse.

steps.q: A client is short of breath. Which position best promotes lung expansion and easier breathing?

opts.text: High-Fowler's (sitting upright)
opts.rat: Sitting upright lowers the diaphragm and allows fuller lung expansion, easing the work of breathing for a dyspneic client.

opts.text: Flat on the back (supine)
opts.rat: Lying flat lets abdominal organs press on the diaphragm and worsens shortness of breath.

opts.text: Trendelenburg (head lower than feet)
opts.rat: Head-down positioning increases pressure on the diaphragm and worsens breathing.

opts.text: Prone (lying face-down)
opts.rat: This is not a routine comfort position for a dyspneic client and can restrict chest movement.

steps.q: Which finding is usually the EARLIEST sign that a client is not getting enough oxygen?

opts.text: Restlessness, anxiety, or a change in behavior
opts.rat: The brain is very sensitive to low oxygen, so restlessness, anxiety, or confusion are often the earliest signs of hypoxia.

opts.text: Bluish lips and nail beds (cyanosis)
opts.rat: Cyanosis is a late sign; oxygen is already significantly low by the time it appears.

opts.text: Clubbing of the fingertips
opts.rat: Clubbing reflects chronic long-term low oxygen, not an acute early change.

opts.text: A drop in body temperature
opts.rat: Temperature change is not a reliable early indicator of hypoxia.

steps.q: Bluish discoloration of the lips and nail beds (cyanosis) is best described as:

opts.text: A late sign of inadequate oxygenation that should be reported promptly
opts.rat: Cyanosis appears after oxygenation has already fallen substantially; it is a late warning sign and needs prompt reporting.

opts.text: A normal finding in most clients
opts.rat: Cyanosis is never a normal expected finding.

opts.text: The first sign of low oxygen
opts.rat: Restlessness and anxiety typically appear before cyanosis; cyanosis is late.

opts.text: A sign the client has too much oxygen
opts.rat: Cyanosis indicates too little oxygen reaching the tissues, not too much.

steps.q: A pulse oximeter is used to measure:

opts.text: The percentage of oxygen saturation in the blood
opts.rat: A pulse oximeter noninvasively estimates the oxygen saturation of the blood (SpO2).

opts.text: The client's blood pressure
opts.rat: Blood pressure is measured with a cuff and sphygmomanometer, not a pulse oximeter.

opts.text: The blood glucose level
opts.rat: Glucose is measured with a glucometer, not a pulse oximeter.

opts.text: The amount of oxygen in the room air
opts.rat: A pulse oximeter reads the client's saturation, not environmental oxygen.

steps.q: To obtain an accurate pulse-oximeter reading on a client's finger, the technician should:

opts.text: Make sure the finger is warm and remove dark nail polish or artificial nails if present
opts.rat: Poor circulation from a cold finger and light-blocking nail polish or artificial nails can cause a falsely low or unreliable reading.

opts.text: Place the probe on a cold, cyanotic finger for the truest value
opts.rat: Cold, poorly perfused fingers give inaccurate readings.

opts.text: Have the client hold their breath during the reading
opts.rat: Breath-holding is unnecessary and can alter the reading.

opts.text: Tape the probe on tightly enough to blanch the fingertip
opts.rat: Excessive pressure impairs blood flow and produces an inaccurate reading.

steps.q: Because oxygen strongly supports combustion, the MOST important safety rule where oxygen is in use is:

opts.text: No smoking or open flames, and post 'Oxygen in Use' precautions
opts.rat: Oxygen makes fires ignite and spread more easily, so eliminating smoking, sparks, and open flames is the priority safety measure.

opts.text: Keep the oxygen tubing tightly coiled under the blanket
opts.rat: Tubing hidden under bedding can kink and can trap heat; it is not the key fire-safety rule.

opts.text: Apply a petroleum-based lubricant to the client's lips and nose
opts.rat: Petroleum (oil-based) products are flammable and should be avoided around oxygen; water-based products are used instead.

opts.text: Turn the oxygen off whenever staff leave the room
opts.rat: Oxygen is a prescribed therapy and is not turned off without an order.

steps.q: A client wearing a nasal cannula reports soreness behind the ears and dryness of the nose. The technician should:

opts.text: Pad the tubing behind the ears and provide water-based lubricant to the nares
opts.rat: Padding pressure points and using a water-soluble moisturizer relieve skin breakdown and dryness without introducing a flammable oil-based product.

opts.text: Apply petroleum jelly generously inside both nostrils
opts.rat: Oil-based products are a fire hazard around oxygen and can be aspirated; use water-based products.

opts.text: Remove the oxygen until the skin heals
opts.rat: Oxygen is a prescribed therapy and is not discontinued without an order.

opts.text: Tighten the cannula strap firmly to stop the movement
opts.rat: Tightening increases pressure and worsens skin breakdown.

steps.q: A low-flow nasal cannula is generally used to deliver oxygen at approximately:

opts.text: 1 to 6 liters per minute
opts.rat: A standard low-flow nasal cannula commonly delivers oxygen in the 1–6 L/min range; higher rates dry the nares and are uncomfortable.

opts.text: 15 to 20 liters per minute
opts.rat: These very high flows are not delivered through a standard nasal cannula.

opts.text: 0 liters per minute
opts.rat: Zero flow would deliver no supplemental oxygen.

opts.text: Any rate the client prefers
opts.rat: Oxygen flow is set to the prescribed rate, not client preference.

steps.q: Compared with a nasal cannula, a simple face mask generally:

opts.text: Delivers a higher concentration of oxygen
opts.rat: A simple mask covers the nose and mouth and delivers a higher oxygen concentration than a low-flow nasal cannula.

opts.text: Delivers less oxygen than a cannula
opts.rat: A mask delivers more, not less, oxygen than a low-flow cannula.

opts.text: Allows the client to eat easily while wearing it
opts.rat: A mask must be removed to eat, unlike a nasal cannula.

opts.text: Is used only during sleep
opts.rat: Mask use is based on oxygen need, not the time of day.

steps.q: The normal resting respiratory rate for an adult is about:

opts.text: 12 to 20 breaths per minute
opts.rat: A normal adult resting respiratory rate is approximately 12–20 breaths per minute.

opts.text: 4 to 8 breaths per minute
opts.rat: This is abnormally slow (bradypnea) for a resting adult and should be reported.

opts.text: 30 to 40 breaths per minute
opts.rat: This is abnormally fast (tachypnea) for a resting adult and should be reported.

opts.text: 60 to 80 breaths per minute
opts.rat: This far exceeds a normal adult rate.

steps.q: Which observation most clearly indicates a client is in respiratory distress and should be reported to the nurse immediately?

opts.text: Use of neck and shoulder (accessory) muscles, nasal flaring, and rapid labored breathing
opts.rat: Accessory-muscle use, nasal flaring, and rapid labored breathing are hallmark signs of increased work of breathing and respiratory distress.

opts.text: Even, quiet breathing at rest
opts.rat: This describes normal, unlabored breathing.

opts.text: Speaking in full sentences without pausing for breath
opts.rat: Being able to speak in full sentences suggests the client is not in acute distress.

opts.text: A regular respiratory rate of 16 per minute
opts.rat: This is within the normal adult range.

steps.q: The main purpose of teaching a client to use an incentive spirometer is to:

opts.text: Encourage slow, deep breaths that expand the lungs and help prevent atelectasis
opts.rat: The incentive spirometer promotes sustained deep inhalation, which re-expands alveoli and helps prevent atelectasis, especially after immobility or surgery.

opts.text: Measure the client's blood oxygen level
opts.rat: Oxygen saturation is measured with a pulse oximeter, not an incentive spirometer.

opts.text: Deliver aerosolized medication to the lungs
opts.rat: Medication is delivered by a nebulizer or inhaler, not an incentive spirometer.

opts.text: Strengthen the client's cough by forcing rapid exhalation
opts.rat: The device emphasizes slow, deep inhalation, not forced exhalation.

steps.q: When coaching a client to use an incentive spirometer, the technician should instruct the client to:

opts.text: Seal the lips around the mouthpiece and inhale slowly and deeply, then hold briefly
opts.rat: A slow, deep inhalation with a brief breath-hold maximizes lung expansion, which is the goal of the device.

opts.text: Blow out into the device as hard and fast as possible
opts.rat: The incentive spirometer is used on inhalation, not forceful exhalation.

opts.text: Take rapid shallow breaths for one minute
opts.rat: Rapid shallow breathing does not expand the alveoli effectively.

opts.text: Use it only when short of breath
opts.rat: It is used regularly on a schedule to prevent complications, not only during distress.

steps.q: Pursed-lip breathing is often taught to clients with chronic lung disease because it:

opts.text: Slows and prolongs exhalation, helping keep airways open and reduce trapped air
opts.rat: Exhaling slowly against pursed lips creates slight back-pressure that keeps small airways open longer, improving air emptying and easing dyspnea.

opts.text: Forces the client to breathe faster
opts.rat: Pursed-lip breathing slows the breathing rate rather than speeding it up.

opts.text: Increases carbon dioxide in the lungs
opts.rat: It helps the client exhale trapped air more effectively, aiding CO2 removal.

opts.text: Replaces the need for prescribed oxygen
opts.rat: It is a breathing technique, not a substitute for prescribed oxygen therapy.

steps.q: To help a client mobilize and clear lung secretions, the technician can encourage the client to:

opts.text: Turn, cough, and deep-breathe regularly and stay well hydrated as allowed
opts.rat: Position changes, coughing, deep breathing, and adequate fluids help loosen and clear secretions and prevent pooling in the lungs.

opts.text: Lie still and breathe as shallowly as possible
opts.rat: Immobility and shallow breathing allow secretions to pool and increase the risk of atelectasis and infection.

opts.text: Avoid all fluids to keep secretions from forming
opts.rat: Adequate hydration thins secretions and makes them easier to clear; restricting fluids thickens them.

opts.text: Suppress every cough with medication
opts.rat: A productive cough clears secretions and should generally be encouraged, not suppressed.

steps.q: A client receiving oxygen becomes newly confused and restless. The technician should FIRST:

opts.text: Check the client and oxygen equipment and report the change to the nurse, as this may signal hypoxia
opts.rat: New confusion and restlessness can be early signs of hypoxia; the technician assesses the client and equipment and promptly reports so oxygenation can be evaluated.

opts.text: Assume the client is seeking attention and ignore it
opts.rat: Dismissing a new mental-status change could miss dangerous hypoxia.

opts.text: Increase the oxygen flow rate independently
opts.rat: Oxygen flow is changed only per order; the technician does not adjust it independently.

opts.text: Apply wrist restraints to keep the client still
opts.rat: Restraints do not address the cause and are never a first response to a mental-status change.

steps.q: Oxygen is considered a medication. This means the technician should:

opts.text: Administer it at the prescribed flow rate and delivery device, and report changes rather than adjusting it independently
opts.rat: Because oxygen is a prescribed therapy, it is given as ordered; changes in the client's status are reported so the licensed team can adjust the order.

opts.text: Change the flow rate whenever the client feels short of breath
opts.rat: Adjusting flow without an order exceeds scope; report the client's status instead.

opts.text: Discontinue it once the client says they feel better
opts.rat: Oxygen is stopped only per order, not on the client's say-so.

opts.text: Share one client's oxygen setup with another client
opts.rat: Equipment and prescribed settings are individual and are never shared between clients.

steps.q: Humidification is often added to oxygen therapy mainly to:

opts.text: Add moisture that helps prevent drying of the airways and nasal passages
opts.rat: Supplemental oxygen is dry; adding humidity reduces drying, cracking, and irritation of the nose and airways.

opts.text: Increase the percentage of oxygen delivered
opts.rat: Humidification adds moisture; it does not raise the oxygen concentration.

opts.text: Sterilize the air the client breathes
opts.rat: Humidifiers moisten air; they do not sterilize it.

opts.text: Replace the need for the client to drink fluids
opts.rat: Airway humidity does not substitute for systemic hydration.

steps.q: When assisting the nurse with oral suctioning of secretions, a key safety principle is to:

opts.text: Apply suction only while withdrawing the catheter and keep each suctioning pass brief
opts.rat: Suctioning only on withdrawal and limiting the duration of each pass reduce mucosal trauma and prevent lowering the client's oxygen level.

opts.text: Apply continuous suction for a full minute at a time
opts.rat: Prolonged suctioning removes oxygen along with secretions and traumatizes tissue.

opts.text: Insert the catheter while actively suctioning
opts.rat: Suctioning on insertion damages mucosa; suction is applied on withdrawal.

opts.text: Reuse the same suction catheter between clients without cleaning
opts.rat: This breaks infection-control principles and can transmit organisms.

steps.q: Which set of changes should the technician report to the licensed nurse as possible worsening of a client's breathing?

opts.text: Faster, more labored breathing with restlessness and a lower pulse-oximeter reading
opts.rat: Rising respiratory rate and effort, new restlessness, and a falling SpO2 together suggest deteriorating oxygenation and need prompt reporting.

opts.text: Even breathing, calm behavior, and a stable oxygen reading
opts.rat: These are reassuring, stable findings.

opts.text: The client comfortably reading a book
opts.rat: This indicates the client is not in distress.

opts.text: A respiratory rate of 14 with pink, warm skin
opts.rat: This is within normal limits with good perfusion.

reference: Aligned to the California BVNPT Psychiatric Technician exam content area: Basic Nursing Care (oxygenation & respiratory care). Written from standard psychiatric-technician and nursing references at an introductory level. Numeric values stated here—normal adult respiratory rate (~12–20/min), low-flow nasal-cannula range (~1–6 L/min), and the general expectation of a normal pulse-oximeter reading—are common reference figures and are marked for faculty confirmation against current facility standards. Oxygen is treated as a prescribed medication administered at the ordered rate/device, consistent with LPT scope; the technician reports changes rather than adjusting flow. Fire-safety (no smoking/open flame, avoid oil-based products near oxygen) and suctioning-on-withdrawal principles are stated at an introductory level. Complements oxygen-safety and pulse-oximetry basics (bnc-core-02) and emergency/choking care (planned BNC-10). No medication doses are asserted. Pending faculty review.
